Smart Substitutions

KITCHEN NOTES / MAKE SUBSTITUTIONS

Swapping herbs without ruining the dish

Hard herbs like the heat early on. Soft herbs prefer to join the party right at the end.

Hard early → Soft late → Taste
Go to the technique ↓Reference

THE SMALL DETAILS THAT HELP

Here's how.

  1. 01

    Identify your herb

    Look at the stem. Is it woody like a twig (rosemary, thyme, oregano)? Or is it soft and green (basil, parsley, cilantro)?

    Look for Woody herbs are "hard". Green, leafy ones are "soft".

  2. 02

    Cook hard herbs early

    Add rosemary or thyme while cooking aromatics (like onions) so the heat can extract their flavor.

    Look for They hold up well to heat and flavor the whole dish over time.

  3. 03

    Fold soft herbs late

    Stir basil, parsley, or cilantro in right before serving.

    Look for Heat destroys their delicate flavor and turns them brown.

A note worth keeping

Know what to look for.

The herbs smell fresh and vibrant when you taste the dish.

Try it in a recipe ↓

AVOID THIS

Swapping a hard herb for a soft herb in the middle of a 30-minute simmer.

Rosemary is aggressive and thrives on heat. Basil is delicate and dies on heat.

TRY THIS INSTEAD

Match the category (hard for hard, soft for soft), or change WHEN you add it.

MAKE SUBSTITUTIONS

Keep the job. Expect a change.

If a recipe wants fresh parsley and you only have dried oregano, use a tiny pinch of the oregano early on, rather than a handful at the end.

Dried vs Fresh?

Dried herbs are concentrated. Use 1 teaspoon of dried herbs for every 1 tablespoon of fresh. Always add dried herbs early in the cooking process so they can rehydrate.
